Variants.Content: Straddling the Volkhov River, Great Novgorod was an autonomous merchant republic in northern Rus. Its wealth came from furs, wax, and timber that merchants carried along the river toward the Baltic and the German trading towns. The Detinets, the fortified kremlin on the riverbank, and the cathedral of St. Sophia overlooked wharves busy with boats and sledges. Free citizens governed the city through the Veche assembly, which gathered at the ringing of the civic bell, and they elected their magistrates, the posadniks. The city hired princes from outside to lead its armies, and it paid tribute to the Mongol khans to spare its streets from the fire that had swept the rest of Rus. Its freedom rested on written charters and on citizens who were ready to gather whenever the bell rang.

Princes served Novgorod under contract as hired commanders, and each contract spelled out the liberties they had to respect. Should a prince violate those liberties, the Veche bell summoned the citizens, who could expel him from the city. Yet against the Teutonic crusaders, Alexander Nevsky's military genius proved irreplaceable, and the city's levies followed him onto Lake Peipus in 1242.
Inscribed birchbark letters serve as everyday correspondence for commoners. From commercial debt ledgers to domestic domestic notes, widespread literacy distinguishes Novgorod from Western serfdoms.
